..
Issued at 211 PM CDT Mon Sep 14 2026

A somewhat conditional severe weather threat remains in the 
forecast for later this afternoon into this evening and 
overnight with the big questions being how unstable we can get 
and how many surface-based storms we can get. Early afternoon 
analysis showed a warm front stretching from north-central KS, 
east-southeast into northeast KS and western MO. This will surge
northward into southeast NE through this afternoon while a 
stream of shortwave energy starts pushing through leading to 
storm development. 18Z KOAX sounding did show a very stout cap, 
though obviously was well north of the boundary. In addition, 
satellite showed quite a bit of cloud cover across the area 
aside from some decent clearing across far southeast NE where 
temperatures had climbed into the mid 80s with dewpoints 
approaching 70. And you don't have to go very far south and west
to see upper 80s and lower 90s. So while much of the area 
remains capped now, the unstable airmass is on the way, though
questions remain as to how far north it'll get.

As for model guidance, there's very good agreement in 
developing a southwest to northeast line of thunderstorms. SPC 
objective mesoanalysis shows sufficient effective layer shear to
yield some supercell structures, but with the line going up 
quickly, think it could become somewhat of a messy storm mode as
we go into the evening. As storms first develop, all severe 
weather hazards would be possible, including tornadoes and even 
a strong tornado, owing to large, looping low level hodographs. 
However, threats should transition to mostly damaging winds and 
heavy rain/flooding with guidance suggesting potential for 
training thunderstorms. In addition, guidance shows 1.75-2" of 
precipitable water with warm cloud depths exceeding 4 km. Low 
level moisture transport will also ramp up this evening and 
overnight and point toward the NE/KS border, where 3+ inches of 
rain fell in some locations last night/this morning. While short
term guidance doesn't produce much precip in those areas, there
remains the possibility that an outflow boundary surges 
southeast out of the line of initial convection owing to line-
parallel 0-3 km shear. This could provide a focus for storm 
development near the NE/KS border as the aforementioned moisture
transport ramps up. Therefore, ended up issuing a Flood Watch 
for much of southeast NE and southwest IA, pairing areas where 
training thunderstorms are most likely with areas that will 
require less rain to see flooding.

The remainder of the week is looking relatively wet with pretty
much daily shower and storm chances. The surface boundary will 
push just south of the area by Tuesday morning, but rain chances
will persist, especially near and south of I-80, as additional 
shortwave energy passes through. While the damaging wind, hail, 
and tornado threat should remain to our south with the higher 
instability, we will see a heavy rain/flooding threat with 
potential for training showers and storms, though still some 
questions as to how far north those will extend. In addition, 
NAEFS precipitable water values look to be in the 1.75-2 inch 
range, good for the 99th+ percentile of climatology for this 
time of year, so anything that does develop will be a pretty 
efficient rain producer. Should it look like heavier precip will
end up in our area, may need to extend part or all of the Flood
Watch. 

A steady stream of shortwave energy will continue Wednesday 
into Thursday while the surface boundary slowly meanders back 
north, eventually reaching SD by Friday. At least on and off 
showers and storms will be possible through that period, with 
potential for repeated rounds of rain to lead to flooding 
concerns. Friday is generally favored to be a drying period, 
though still looking at 20- 30 percent chance of rain in the 
afternoon with a few various ensemble members a little slower 
with the northward advancement of the front. However, any dry 
period looks to be short-lived as a cold front pushes in from 
the northwest for the weekend and gives us continued 30-50% 
chances of rain. Machine learning severe weather guidance keeps
severe weather potential below (under 5%) through this active 
period, though again, potential heavy rain and flooding will 
remain a concern with each successive round.

Otherwise, temperatures may be a bit of a roller coaster 
through the week and will hinge on precipitation on a given day.
Currently, upper 60s and 70s are favored Tuesday and Wednesday 
before the front moves back north and marks a return to the 80s 
Thursday and Friday. Behind the weekend cold front, expect to be
back down in the 70s to lower 80s. But again, lots of moving 
parts, so confidence in exact temperatures on a given day is 
relatively low.
